# Smriti: private AI agents and workflows that cite their sources
URL: https://safearly.com/

Smriti · open-source institutional memory Private AI agents that cite their sources. Connect your documents, sites, APIs and databases. Give every team agents and workflows that answer with citations checked line by line, see only what the person asking may see, and run on your own hardware, with or without a GPU. Self-host in 5 minutes View on GitHub Apache-2.0 · No account, no telemetry · Your models, your network Policy desk · agent How many days of notice does a supplier need to end the contract, and has that changed? Searched 4 sources you can open Found the clause and its amendment Checked 3 of 3 sentences Since the 2025 amendment, either party may end the contract with 60 days' written notice [1] . Before that, the notice period was 30 days [2] . ✓ verified as you 2 sources $ git clone https://github.com/physicsisawesome7/smriti $ cd smriti && ./install.sh # detects your GPU, or runs on CPU Deploy your way Where your data already lives. Deployment guide → ◻ A laptop, no GPU The CPU profile answers with verified extracts and computes table maths in code. Useful from the first minute, on any machine with Docker. ◼ One consumer GPU Profiles for 6, 12, 16 and 24 GB cards pick an open-weight model, embeddings and a reranker that fit, and leave room for the cache. ▦ Your servers PostgreSQL, Qdrant and S3-compatible storage, with stateless API replicas and separate ingestion workers that scale on their own. ⛨ Fully offline Once installed, nothing needs the internet. Models are open weights you host, and the default ones are Apache-2.0. Outbound requests pass an egress guard. The platform From scattered documents to work that gets done. Knowledge Connect Websites, uploads, folders, feeds, REST APIs, SQL and MCP servers. Every change becomes a new version. 8 source types · scheduled sync · change alerts Answers Ask Hybrid search filtered to the asker, the version in force, amendments attached, and every sentence checked. as-of dates · table maths · abstains when unsure Agents Delegate Assistants with their own instructions, sources and tools, from cited lookup to research and tool use. 4 kinds · 10 tool types · approvals Workflows Automate Chain agents, conditions, code, loops and human sign-off on a visual canvas, with the same guarantees. 9 step types · templates · step limit Applications Reach The web app, a website widget, Slack, Telegram, Discord, an OpenAI-compatible API and an MCP server. one identity rule everywhere How every answer is made, whether it comes from the app, an agent, a workflow or a chat bot. Why teams pick Smriti Built for answers someone will act on. One question, three people, three answers: each built only from what that person may read. Typical AI document assistant Smriti Wrong answers Shown as written, with a citation at the end Each sentence checked against the passage it cites, numbers included. Replaced by a verified extract, or Smriti says what is missing. Who sees what An assistant account that can read everything Every agent, workflow, widget and bot acts as the person asking. Checked during search and again before display. Changing documents The latest upload wins Versions, supersessions and amendments tracked. Ask "as of" any date. Personal data Sent to the model as is Masked by role before any model or external tool, restored for the person on screen. Built on Saaf . Agent actions The model decides Changes wait for approval. After reading outside content they always do, so injected text can't trigger a write. Running cost Every question calls a large model Lookups and table questions skip the model. A guarded cache, compact prompts and load shedding keep one GPU busy, not overloaded. Without a model Nothing works Search, cited extracts, table maths and research still work, so an offline install answers on day one. Release gates Every release has to pass these first. 14 / 14 golden questions, including permission, superseded-version and unanswerable traps 0 of 102 leakage probes returned a document the person may not see 6 / 6 red-team attacks stopped: direct, indirect and multilingual injection, escalation, extraction 100% planted defects found by the coded document validators, with no false alarms Measured on Smriti's small synthetic demo corpus with the built-in offline components. These numbers show the gates work; real accuracy has to be measured on your own documents, and the same gates run on your golden set. Applications One memory, every team. All applications → Customer support Answers from manuals, release notes and past tickets, embedded in your help centre, with personal data kept out of the model. See how → Internal knowledge HR, IT and policy questions in Slack or the intranet, answered as each employee, so private files stay private. See how → Legal and contracts Clause lookup with amendments in force, comparisons across agreements, and sign-off before anything leaves the team. See how → Finance, risk and compliance Regulations and circulars that change, watched for you, with "what changed" notes and the documents each change affects. See how → Engineering and product Specs, runbooks and API docs in one place, with an agent that can also query read-only data and run analysis code. See how → Public sector Rules, orders and notices with version history, on infrastructure you control, with an audit trail for every answer. See how → From the blog Learn how trustworthy AI answers are built. All posts → Trust Security you can inspect, not just read about. Security model → Identity Access is checked twice, in code. Administrators configure the system without reading its content. Audit A hash-chained log of every answer, tool call, approval and access decision, verifiable from the CLI. Guardrails Injection scanning, sentence verification, personal-data masking and human approval for anything that changes data. Open code Apache-2.0, with the release gates and the leakage suite in the repository. Read it, run it, change it. Questions Frequently asked. Is Smriti really open source? Yes. The whole platform is Apache-2.0, including agents, workflows, integrations and the release gates. There is no paid tier hidden behind the open one. Safearly offers help with pilots and deployments. Which models does it use? Any OpenAI-compatible server, chosen per task. The installer starts open-weight Qwen3 models with matching embeddings and a reranker sized for your GPU. With no model at all, it still searches, quotes verified extracts and computes tables. Does any data leave our network? Not unless you connect something that sends it. Models run on your hardware. Outbound requests from crawlers and tools pass an egress guard, personal data is masked before anything goes to an external tool, and chat-app replies are masked by default. How is this different from a chatbot over our PDFs? Three things: answers are verified sentence by sentence and withheld when they fail; access is enforced for the person asking on every surface; and document versions and amendments are tracked, so you get the rule in force, not just the newest file. Can we put it in our own app or website? Yes. Add a widget with one script tag, call any agent through an OpenAI-compatible API, connect assistants such as Claude or IDE agents over MCP, or put agents in Slack, Telegram and Discord. Is there a hosted version? Not yet. Smriti is built to run on infrastructure you control. If you'd like help with a pilot, write to us . Give your organisation a memory it can trust. Run the demo on your laptop today, or talk to us about a pilot on your own documents. Self-host in 5 minutes Plan a pilot Star on GitHub

# Agents · Smriti · Safearly
URL: https://safearly.com/agents

Agents Agents that cite their work and know their limits. Build an assistant in minutes: instructions, sources, tools. Whoever uses it sees only what they're allowed to see. Every answer is checked against what its tools returned, and anything that would change data waits for a person. Build your first agent Browse the gallery IT helpdesk · agentic My laptop VPN keeps dropping. Can you open a ticket? search · "VPN drops" → 3 passages helpdesk.get_known_issues → 1 match Approval needed Helpdesk wants to run create_ticket (title="VPN disconnects every few minutes"). Approve Decline acts as you changes need approval Four kinds Pick how much the agent does on its own. Classic Cited lookup Answers from the agent's sources through the full pipeline: version rules, "as of" dates, amendments and table maths. No model needed for lookups. Agentic Uses tools Decides which tools to call, reads the results and answers with citations to them. Without a model, a rule planner still searches, reads links and calculates. Research Plans and verifies Splits a broad question into two to five parts, answers each with its own verification, and merges them into one cited report. Workflow Follows a process A graph of agent steps, conditions, code, loops and approvals that runs in order. Workflows → The agentic loop. Every tool result becomes a citable passage, and actions that change data wait for the asker. Gallery Start from an agent that already works. How to build one → Classic Support assistant Answers customers and agents from manuals, release notes and FAQs, and says when the docs don't cover it. Sources manuals, release notes Tools search Does version 4.2 support single sign-on? Classic Policy and HR desk Leave, travel, expenses and conduct rules, quoting the policy in force on the date asked. Sources HR and finance policies Tools search What was the travel allowance before the April revision? Agentic Contract analyst Finds the clause, applies amendments, and does the arithmetic exactly, citing where every figure came from. Sources contracts, amendments Tools search, calculator, files What is the liability cap, and what is 5% of 4,80,00,000? Research Research brief Turns a broad question into a short, cited brief for a decision-maker, one verified section per sub-question. Sources everything you can see Tools search What changed in our data-retention rules this year, and who is affected? Agentic Data analyst Writes and runs Python in a sandbox with no network to analyse tables, then hands back a CSV or chart. Sources reports, exports Tools search, Python, files Make a CSV of last quarter's incidents by team. Agentic IT helpdesk Checks known issues in your ticketing API and opens a ticket only after the person approves it. Sources runbooks, IT policies Tools search, REST API My VPN keeps dropping. Open a ticket. Agentic Web researcher Searches the web through your own search engine, with personal data removed from the query before it leaves. Sources library and the web Tools web search, read page What did the regulator publish this month about cloud outsourcing? Agentic Reporting assistant Answers numeric questions with read-only SQL against a reporting database, with a row cap and table notes. Sources data dictionary Tools database (read-only) How many orders were refunded in September, by region? Tools Ten kinds of tools, each with its own limits. Tool reference → Tool What it does Built-in safety Search the library Permission-aware search with version rules, limited to the agent's sources Filtered to the asker Calculator Exact arithmetic A real parser, never eval Read a web page Fetches one URL Egress guard; treated as untrusted Web search Self-hosted SearxNG, Brave or Tavily Personal data masked in the query Run Python Analysis and file generation No network, read-only root, non-root, memory and time limits Create a file Markdown, CSV, JSON, HTML or text Always a download, never rendered Skills Coded checks for your domain Their own grant checks REST API Operations from an OpenAPI spec Writes hidden unless allowed, then always approved MCP server Every tool on a server Non-read-only tools need approval Database SELECT queries Read-only transaction and a row cap Guarantees Why the answers can be trusted. Acts as the asker An agent built by someone with wide access never shows more to someone with less. Its sources only narrow what is searched. Every result is citable Tool results become numbered passages. The answer is verified sentence by sentence against them, and a failing one is replaced or withheld. Personal data stays masked Masked before the model sees the question or a tool result, and before anything goes to an external tool, then restored on screen. Injected text can't act After a run reads outside content, every action that changes data waits for approval, whatever the agent's setting. Everywhere Share it, schedule it, call it. Share and publish Keep it private, share it with everyone or with chosen roles, as a draft or published. Shared conversations hide answers whose sources the viewer can't open. Run on a schedule A cron expression and a question. Published agents run as their owner and post the result to a conversation. Use from code Per-agent keys work with the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so any SDK or chat client can call an agent and get its sources. curl https://smriti.example/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-smriti-…" \ -d '{"model": "agent/contract-analyst", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is the liability cap?"}]}'

# Workflows · Smriti · Safearly
URL: https://safearly.com/workflows

Workflows Draw the process. Keep the guarantees. Some work is more than one question. A workflow chains agents, conditions, variables, code and human sign-off into one run on a visual canvas. Every agent step still acts as the person running it, cites its sources and masks personal data. Build a workflow See examples ▶ Start query ◎ Draft answer research → draft ⑂ Found one? len(draft) > 0 ✋ Sign-off approve / decline ■ Released {{ draft }} ■ Held back "Not released" The "sign-off before release" template, as it looks in the builder. Building blocks Nine steps, connected on a canvas. ◎ AI agent A classic, agentic or research agent on a templated prompt, with its own tools. Its cited answer goes into a variable. ⑂ If / else Conditions checked in order; the first true one wins, otherwise the else branch. ≔ Set state Variables from expressions such as float(amount) * 0.05 , without calling a model. {} Code Python in a sandbox with no network. It reads the workflow's variables and prints a value back. ✋ Human approval Pauses until the person running it approves or declines, and branches on the answer. ↻ Loop One agent prompt for each item in a list, with the answers collected and their citations merged. Plus Start , End (renders the final answer from a template) and Note (a comment on the canvas). Examples Workflows teams run. Workflow docs → Template Sign-off before release A research agent drafts a cited answer; a reviewer approves it before it goes into official correspondence. research agent if found human approval release or hold Template Answer a questionnaire Paste a security questionnaire or RFP. Each question is answered with citations and collected into one reply. split the questions loop: cited answer combine Template Route by topic Questions about money go to an agent with a calculator; everything else to cited lookup. if / else on the question agentic or classic agent end Example Ticket triage Classify a request, answer it from runbooks if possible, and open a ticket through your API only after approval. classic agent: try to answer if no answer agentic: create ticket (approval) Example Weekly change digest Every Monday, summarise what changed in watched sources and tabulate it for each team. schedule: Mon 09:00 research agent: what changed code: build the table Example Threshold check Pull a figure from a contract, compare it with your limit, and escalate to a person when it is over. agent: find the amount set state: number(answer) if over limit → approval Variables and expressions Logic without a scripting engine. Prompts and outputs are templates with {{ }} . Conditions use a small expression language that Smriti parses itself. Attribute access, imports and unknown functions are rejected when you save, so a workflow can't reach anything it shouldn't. len(answer) > 0 and contains(answer, 'clause') float(amount) * 0.05 [strip(q) for q in split(query, ';')] join(pluck(answers, 'answer'), '\n\n') 'urgent' if matches(lower(query), 'today|now') else 'normal' Safe by construction What still holds inside a workflow. Acts as the runner Every agent step searches only what the person running the workflow may see. One citation list Citations from every step are renumbered into one list, and the final answer is scored against them. Approvals pause it all A human step, or a tool action inside an agent step, pauses the whole run. Only the runner can approve. Bounded and explained A run stops after 50 steps. Any failure ends with an answer naming the step that failed, and why. Validated before it can run Saving checks the graph: one start, at least one end, every output connected, every step reachable, valid variable names and safe expressions. Errors read like "'If / else' (else) is not connected to a next step".

URL: https://safearly.com/applications

Applications One memory, wherever people work. Smriti's agents and workflows run in its own web app, inside your website, in chat apps and in your code. Wherever they run, the same rule applies: the answer is checked, and it never shows more than the person behind it may see. Where it runs What teams use it for Where it runs Seven ways in. Integration docs → ◎ Web app Ask with evidence and a trace, build agents and workflows, browse versions and diffs, approve drafts, check the audit chain. ◱ Website widget One script tag adds a chat bubble with streamed, cited answers. It runs only on sites you allow, as you or as the signed-in user. # Slack Mention the app or message it. Answers arrive in the thread, approvals are buttons only the asker can press. ✈ Telegram A bot for staff in the field. Each chat continues one conversation, with personal data masked in replies. ◆ Discord An app with an /ask command, with every request verified by Discord's signature. {} OpenAI-compatible API Point any SDK or chat client at /v1/chat/completions and choose an agent as the model. ⇄ MCP server Let assistants such as Claude or IDE agents search Smriti, with the caller's permissions fixed when it starts. ✓ Same rules everywhere Every surface states who it answers as. Chat-app replies are masked, and answers citing confidential documents stay in Smriti. What teams use it for Six common starting points. # Smriti documentation · Safearly
URL: https://safearly.com/docs

Smriti documentation Smriti is open-source institutional memory. It reads your documents and the sites and systems you depend on, keeps every version, and answers with citations it has checked. Agents and workflows built on it act as the person asking, and everything runs on hardware you control. Quickstart → Install, open the demo and ask your first question in five minutes. Install and deploy → Hardware profiles, configuration, scaling and offline installs. Agents and tools → Build assistants with instructions, sources, tools and approvals. Workflows → Chain agents, conditions, code, loops and human sign-off. Integrations → Website widget, Slack, Telegram and Discord. API, MCP and CLI → REST, OpenAI-compatible endpoints, MCP and the command line. What Smriti is for Organisations run on documents that change: policies, contracts, manuals, regulations, orders. People need the version that applies, need to see only what they're allowed to, and need to trust the answer enough to act on it. Smriti is built around those three needs: Verified answers. Every sentence is checked against the passage it cites, numbers included. Answers that fail are replaced by a verified extract, or Smriti says what is missing. Access that holds. Permissions are checked during search and again before display, and every agent, workflow and integration acts as the person asking. Versions and amendments. Smriti knows which document supersedes or amends which, and can answer "as of" any date. How the docs are organised Get started : run it and find your way around. Core concepts : how answers, knowledge and access work. Build : agents, workflows and integrations. Reference : endpoints, commands, limits and answers to common questions. The versioned reference for each release lives in the repository, next to the code. Each page here links to it.

# Quickstart · Smriti docs
URL: https://safearly.com/docs/quickstart

Quickstart Run Smriti on your machine, open the demo organisation, and see verified answers, access control and versions at work. It takes about five minutes. 1. Install You need Docker. A GPU is optional: without one, Smriti uses its CPU profile and answers with verified extracts. git clone https://github.com/physicsisawesome7/smriti cd smriti ./install.sh # Linux, WSL2, macOS powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File install.ps1 # Windows The installer checks Docker and GPU access, picks a hardware profile from your graphics memory, writes .env , starts the stack and waits until every model server is ready. No Docker? With Python 3.11 or later: pip install -e ".[dev]" , then smriti --data-dir data serve --seed . It starts on http://127.0.0.1:8000 with the demo seeded. 2. Ask a question Open the app. Under Viewing as , pick a person: the demo directory has people with different roles. Ask: What is the period for submitting the performance guarantee under clause 16.1? You get an answer with numbered citations, the steps Smriti took, and a verification score. Open a citation to see the passage it came from. 3. Ask it as of a date Ask the same question as of an earlier date. The answer changes to the text that applied then, because the demo includes an amendment that came into force later. 4. Switch people Ask about a restricted document as different people. One sees it in full, one sees it with names masked, and one is told nothing relevant was found. The same holds for every agent, workflow and integration. 5. Build an agent Open Agents , start from a template, and use Try it to run it before saving. Then open Start from a workflow and run the sign-off template to see a human approval step. 6. Put it on a page As a knowledge manager, publish an agent, open Agents → Integrations , add a website widget for this address, and press Try it on this page . Every document in the demo is synthetic. To use your own documents, roles and sources, see Install and deploy .

# Install and deploy · Smriti docs
URL: https://safearly.com/docs/install

Install and deploy One command brings up the whole stack on one machine. The same code scales out to separate databases, vector stores and model servers. What runs smriti-api : the web app and API. Stateless; run several processes. smriti-worker : ingestion jobs and scheduled crawls. PostgreSQL : documents, versions, conversations and the audit log. Qdrant : dense and sparse vectors. Embeddings and reranker : served by Text Embeddings Inference. LLM : vLLM serving an AWQ model with prefix caching. Optional. Sandbox : an isolated service for agents' Python, on an internal-only network. Hardware profiles Profile Card Model Encoders cpu none none: verified extractive answers CPU gpu-6gb 6 GB laptop cards Qwen3-4B AWQ CPU gpu-12gb 12 GB Qwen3-4B AWQ GPU gpu-16gb 16 GB Qwen3-8B AWQ GPU gpu-24gb 24 GB Qwen3-14B AWQ GPU Each profile file shows its memory arithmetic. Force one with ./install.sh --profile gpu-12gb --reconfigure . The default models, embeddings and reranker are Apache-2.0. The 12 and 16 GB profiles are sized from documented arithmetic and should be benchmarked on your card. Why it is cheap to run Lookups and table questions are answered by verified quotes or by code, without the model. A guarded cache reuses verified answers for people with identical access. Evidence is compressed to the relevant sentences, under a token cap. Prompts open with a fixed prefix that the model server caches. Admission control serves the verified extract instead of queueing when the GPU is saturated. Measure on your hardware with smriti bench --concurrency 8 --requests 200 (add --no-cache for the GPU path only). Prometheus metrics are at /api/metrics . Configuration Everything is set in .env . Common changes: Change How A different model LLM_MODEL=… , then restart the llm service A model on another machine, Ollama or llama.cpp SMRITI_CHAT_URL and SMRITI_CHAT_MODEL pointing at any OpenAI-compatible endpoint Serve your network SMRITI_BIND=0.0.0.0 behind a TLS reverse proxy Real logins SMRITI_AUTH=token with SMRITI_API_TOKENS , behind your SSO proxy More API processes SMRITI_WORKERS=4 Public address for bots and webhooks SMRITI_PUBLIC_URL=https://smriti.example Web search for agents add search to COMPOSE_PROFILES and set SMRITI_SEARXNG_URL Turn code execution off SMRITI_SANDBOX_URL= (empty) Your own documents and roles Each organisation is a pack : a folder of YAML and Markdown for documents, roles, sources, schemas, guardrails, glossary and skills. Copy the demo pack, edit it, and point SMRITI_PACKS at it. Check a pack without starting anything: smriti validate-pack packs/tenants/your-org Scaling out API processes are stateless, and ingestion jobs are database rows that any number of workers claim atomically. For production, use PostgreSQL ( SMRITI_DATABASE_URL ), Qdrant ( SMRITI_VECTOR_BACKEND=qdrant ) and S3-compatible storage ( SMRITI_BLOB_URL=s3://… ). Offline installs Run the installer once online so the model cache fills, then set HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 . Move container images with docker save and docker load . After that, nothing needs the internet. Troubleshooting Containers can't see the GPU : install the NVIDIA Container Toolkit on Linux, or update the driver and Docker Desktop (WSL2 backend) on Windows. The model server runs out of memory : lower LLM_MAX_NUM_SEQS or LLM_MAX_MODEL_LEN , or LLM_GPU_MEMORY_UTILIZATION by 0.05. Newest GPUs without matching kernels : set VLLM_IMAGE to a build that supports your card.

---

# How Smriti works · Smriti docs
URL: https://safearly.com/docs/concepts

How Smriti works Every answer goes through the same pipeline, whether it comes from the web app, an agent, a workflow or a chat bot. The path of a question The pipeline every answer goes through. Guard the input. The question is scanned for injection attempts, and personal data is masked with Saaf . Expand. Abbreviations and synonyms from the organisation's glossary widen the search. Search with the access filter. Hybrid keyword and vector search runs with the asker's permissions as a filter. Re-check access. Every result is checked again against the source of truth before it can be used. Apply version rules. Superseded text is dropped, and amendments in force on the date asked are attached to the clause they change. Rerank and write. The best passages are reranked. Totals over tables are computed in code. Otherwise a model writes an answer, or a verified extract is used. Verify. Each sentence is checked against the passages it cites. Answer or abstain. A failing answer is replaced by a verified extract, or Smriti says what is missing. Record. A trace of the run and an entry in the audit log. Verification An answer is split into sentences. Each factual sentence must cite passages. Its support is the share of its content words found in those passages, and every number, amount, percentage and clause id must appear verbatim in a cited passage. Uncited factual sentences count as unsupported. The score is shown with the answer and drives abstention. Versions and amendments Documents are linked by supersession and amendment relations. A question can carry an "as of" date. Retrieval returns the text in force on that date, and a clause always arrives together with every amendment that applies, so the answer leads with the amended text. People, roles and grants The person asking is a principal with roles. Roles give grants ( view , upload , curate , administer , audit ) and a scope: which divisions, projects, classifications and document types they may read, and which personal data they may see unmasked. An administrator configures the system without being a reader of its content. Packs An organisation is configured as layered packs. Platform defaults load first, then an optional vertical pack for an industry, then the tenant pack: models per task, roles, sources, document schemas, guardrails, glossary, skills and evaluation sets. Skills Skills are coded domain checks: an extractor, rules written in code, and an explanation. Thresholds are read from the document in force, never hard-coded, and results become drafts that go through maker-checker approval. Evaluation and release gates smriti eval gate runs a golden question set, a leakage suite that probes every person against every document they may not see, a red-team set, and the skills' planted-defect tests. CI blocks a release when any gate fails. Run the same gates on your own golden set.

---

# Knowledge and sources · Smriti docs
URL: https://safearly.com/docs/knowledge

Knowledge and sources Smriti's memory comes from sources you connect in the Ingest view. Each one has a test run, its own access and schedule settings, and background jobs you can watch and cancel. Source types Kind What it reads Website A whole site from a start page, scoped by path or domain, with linked PDF, Office and ZIP files. Honours robots.txt and a per-host rate limit. Web page or file link One URL. A re-sync stores a new version when it changes. Upload files Drag and drop, up to 200 MB each, ZIP archives unpacked. Parsed in the background. REST / JSON API Records from an HTTP API, with auth, pagination and field mapping, or a linked file per record. Database (SQL) One read-only query: each row a document, or the result as one table for exact totals. MCP server Every resource on a server, or the result of one tool call. RSS, Atom or sitemap Each linked page or document, with its title and date. Server folder Files under an allowed folder, such as a mounted shared drive. Adding a source Add source : pick a kind, or start from a demo preset. Test connection : a dry run that finds a few items and parses the first ones. Nothing is stored. Save & run : queues a job for the worker. Jobs : live progress, a result for each item linked to the library, a log, and Cancel. Re-runs are cheap: unchanged content is recognised by hash and skipped, changed content becomes a new version, and removed items are kept or marked removed. Access and schedules Every source sets the sensitivity, divisions, projects, need-to-know groups and document type of what it brings in, plus a cron schedule and what to do when an item disappears. If the same content arrives from two sources with different access, the stricter rule wins. Watching for change When a watched source changes, Smriti writes a "what changed" note and lists the documents that cite the changed text, filtered to what each reader may open. Safety Egress guard : every request and redirect is checked, blocking loopback, cloud-metadata and reserved addresses and Smriti's own internal services. Credentials : encrypted at rest and never returned by the API. SQL : a single SELECT, in a read-only transaction, with a row cap. MCP : network transports only, so a source can't run programs on the host. Audit : every create, change, run, preview and cancel is logged. Scanned pages without a text layer are flagged as low-confidence and queued. OCR and advanced layout parsing are plug-in points, not bundled.

---

# Security and access · Smriti docs
URL: https://safearly.com/docs/security

Security and access Smriti assumes the model will sometimes be wrong or be fooled, and puts the guarantees in code around it. Access control Access is enforced before the model reads anything, not by filtering its answer. Two enforcement points. A filter during search, then a bulk re-check against the source of truth before anything is used. Administrators are not readers. Configuring the system doesn't grant access to its content. Agents act as the asker. Agents, workflows, widgets and bots search only what the person behind them may see. An agent's sources narrow access, never widen it. Leakage suite. Every person is probed against every document they may not see, in CI. Personal data Personal data is masked by category and role, using Saaf : before a model sees a question, document passage or tool result, and before anything is sent to an external tool. People who may see a value see it restored. The index holds masked text by default. Prompt injection Inputs are scored for injection, with an optional guard model for unsure cases. Documents and tool results are treated as data, scanned and flagged. After a run has read outside content (web, API, MCP, SQL), every action that changes data waits for human approval, whatever the agent's setting. Actions and approvals Agents ask before changing data by default. REST write operations are hidden until a curator allows them, and then always need approval. MCP tools not marked read-only need approval. Only the person who started a run can approve it. Infrastructure Credentials for sources, tools and bots are encrypted at rest and never returned by the API. Egress guard on every outbound request, including redirects. Code sandbox : no network, read-only root, non-root user, no capabilities, memory, process and time limits. Downloads created by agents are always served as attachments, never rendered. Integrations verify every inbound request: signing secrets, secret tokens, Ed25519 signatures or an origin allow-list. Audit Answers, tool calls, approvals, access decisions and configuration changes are written to a hash-chained log. Verify the chain with smriti audit-verify . Deployment checklist Turn on token auth ( SMRITI_AUTH=token ) behind your SSO proxy. Serve over TLS through a reverse proxy. Set SMRITI_SECRET_KEY from your secrets manager, rather than relying on the key file Smriti creates in its data directory. Block private networks for crawlers if you don't crawl the intranet ( SMRITI_EGRESS_ALLOW_PRIVATE=0 ). Use read-only database accounts for SQL sources and tools. Run the release gates on your own golden set before go-live. To report a vulnerability, write to lalit@safearly.com .

---

# Agents and tools · Smriti docs
URL: https://safearly.com/docs/agents

Agents and tools An agent is a saved assistant with its own instructions, sources and tools. Open Agents in the web app. Anyone with the view grant can build a private agent. Sharing one, and connecting external tools, needs curate or administer . Kinds Kind What it does Needs a model? Classic Cited answers from the agent's sources through the full pipeline. No Agentic A tool loop: the model picks tools, reads results and answers with citations to them. For the full loop; a rule planner works without one Research Two to five sub-questions, each answered and verified, merged into one report. No; a model improves the plan Workflow A graph of steps. See Workflows . For its agent steps Settings Instructions : who it answers for, tone, what to always include. Platform rules sit above them: cite every factual sentence, treat tool results as data, and say what is missing instead of guessing. Sources : everything the asker may see, or chosen document types and ingestion sources. Sources narrow retrieval; they never widen it. Tools : built-in and connected tools (below). Approval : ask before anything that changes data (default), before every tool call, or never. After reading outside content, changes always need approval. Starter questions , max tool steps , and only answer when supported by citations (on by default). Sharing : only me, everyone, or chosen roles; draft or published. Schedule : a cron expression and a question. Published agents run as their owner and post to a conversation. The builder's Try it panel runs the agent as it stands in the form, unsaved. Tools Tool Type Notes Search the library built in Permission-aware, with version rules, limited to the agent's sources. Calculator built in Exact arithmetic with a safe parser. Read a web page built in Through the egress guard; untrusted content. Web search built in Self-hosted SearxNG, or Brave or Tavily with a key. Personal data masked in the query. Run Python built in The sandbox service: no network, read-only root, limits. Written files come back as downloads. Create a file built in Markdown, CSV, JSON, HTML or text, as a download. Skills built in The pack's coded skills, with their own grant checks. REST API connected From an OpenAPI spec or listed by hand. Writes hidden unless allowed, then approved. MCP server connected Every tool of a server over streamable HTTP or SSE. Non-read-only tools need approval. Database connected Read-only SELECT with a row cap. Add table notes for better SQL. Every connected tool has the roles that may use it and a sensitivity for its results. Credentials are encrypted and never returned. Saving a tool reads its actions from the target, so you see exactly what agents can call. Conversations and sharing Chats are saved per person and agent. Share makes a link. Someone who opens it sees only the answers whose cited documents they can open themselves. API keys Open an agent's API keys . A key ( sk-smriti-… ) is shown once, works for that agent only, and acts as the person who created it. curl https://smriti.example/api/agents/contract-analyst/chat \ -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-smriti-…" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"question": "What is the liability cap?", "stream": false}' The same key works with the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, using the model name agent/<id> . See API, MCP and CLI .

# Workflows · Smriti docs
URL: https://safearly.com/docs/workflows

Workflows A workflow is an agent built as a graph of steps. Open Agents → New agent , choose Workflow and draw it on the canvas, or start from a template under Start from a workflow . It is saved, shared, scheduled, given API keys and chatted with like any other agent. Steps Step What it does Outputs Start Every run begins here with query and chat_history . one AI agent A classic, agentic or research agent on a templated prompt. Its cited answer goes into the output variable and last . one If / else Checks conditions in order and follows the first that is true. one per condition, plus else Set state Sets variables from expressions. one Code Python in the sandbox. Variables are in a dict called state ; print JSON on the last line to return a value. one Human approval Pauses until the runner approves or declines. approved, declined Loop One agent prompt per list item (up to 20), collecting [{item, answer}] . one End Its template becomes the answer. none Note A comment. Never runs. none Every step also writes its result to node_<id> . On the canvas, drag a step to move it, drag from an output port onto another step to connect, click to edit, and press Delete to remove the selection. Templates and expressions Prompts, approval messages and End outputs are templates: Release this answer?\n\n{{ draft }} . Conditions and Set state take expressions: len(answer) > 0 and contains(answer, 'clause') float(amount) * 0.05 [strip(q) for q in split(query, ';')] join(pluck(answers, 'answer'), '\n\n') 'urgent' if matches(lower(query), 'today|immediately') else 'normal' The language is a whitelisted subset of Python expressions, parsed and walked by Smriti, never passed to eval . Allowed: literals, variables, arithmetic, comparisons, and / or / not , in , indexing, conditional expressions, simple list comprehensions, and the functions abs bool contains default float int join json keys len lower matches max min number pluck round split startswith str strip upper . Anything else is rejected when the workflow is saved. Guarantees Every agent step acts as the person running the workflow, masks personal data and verifies its answer. Citations from all steps are renumbered into one list, and the final answer is scored against them. A Human approval step, or a tool action inside an agent step that needs approval, pauses the whole run. Inside a Loop, such actions are skipped and recorded. A run stops after 50 steps. Errors end the run with an answer naming the failing step. Saving validates the graph: one Start, at least one End, every output connected, every step reachable, nothing into Start, valid names and safe expressions. API Workflows are agents with "kind": "workflow" and a graph : { "name": "Sign-off flow", "kind": "workflow", "graph": { "nodes": [ {"id": "start", "type": "start"}, {"id": "draft", "type": "agent", "data": {"kind": "research", "prompt": "{{ query }}", "output": "draft"}}, {"id": "ok", "type": "approval", "data": {"message": "Release?\n\n{{ draft }}"}}, {"id": "yes", "type": "end", "data": {"output": "{{ draft }}"}}, {"id": "no", "type": "end", "data": {"output": "Held back."}} ], "edges": [ {"source": "start", "target": "draft"}, {"source": "draft", "target": "ok"}, {"source": "ok", "target": "yes", "handle": "approved"}, {"source": "ok", "target": "no", "handle": "declined"} ] } } Run it with POST /api/agents/{id}/chat , or try an unsaved graph with POST /api/agents/preview . A paused run returns status: awaiting_approval and a run_id ; continue with POST /api/runs/{run_id}/approve?approve=true .

# Integrations · Smriti docs
URL: https://safearly.com/docs/integrations

Integrations Open Agents → Integrations to put a published agent in a web page, Slack, Telegram or Discord. Creating one needs curate or administer and an agent you can edit. Each has a setup panel with the steps, embed code or webhook URL, and test buttons. Who an integration answers as Mode On Behaviour Fixed all Answers as the person who created it. Right for public help desks over public documents. Signed-in users widget The host site's server signs a short-lived token for the logged-in user; the widget answers as them, and approvals work. Mapped people Slack, Telegram, Discord Chat-app user ids mapped to Smriti users by an administrator. Unmapped people are refused. Checks on answers that leave Smriti Personal data is masked in replies to chat apps, which store every message. On by default. Classified answers stay home. An answer citing documents above the limit (default internal ) becomes a link back to Smriti, and the event is audited. Approvals are buttons only the person who asked can press. Inbound requests are verified : Slack signing secret with a 5-minute window, Telegram secret token, Discord Ed25519 signature, widget origin allow-list and rate limit. The origin check stops other websites from embedding your widget, not a script that copies the URL. A fixed widget is public to anyone who can reach Smriti; use signed-in users for anything private. Website widget <script src="https://smriti.example/widget.js" data-smriti-widget="wg_…" data-host="https://smriti.example" async></script> Optional: data-user-token (signed widgets), data-position="left" , data-open="true" . In JavaScript: SmritiWidget.open() , .close() , .ask(text) , .setUserToken(token) . It renders in a shadow root, streams cited answers and keeps the conversation for the tab. Signing a user on your server: import hashlib, hmac, time exp = int(time.time()) + 3600 sig = hmac.new(SIGNING_KEY.encode(), f"{user_id}.{exp}".encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest() token = f"{user_id}.{exp}.{sig}" Slack Create an app at api.slack.com/apps with the bot scopes app_mentions:read , chat:write and im:history , and install it. Paste the bot token and signing secret into Smriti. Set the Event Subscriptions and Interactivity URLs to the webhook URL, subscribed to app_mention and message.im . Telegram Create a bot with @BotFather and paste its token. Press Connect webhook . Discord Paste the Application ID, Public Key and bot token. Set the Interactions Endpoint URL to the webhook URL, then press Register /ask . Invite the app with the applications.commands scope. Bots need Smriti reachable from the internet at SMRITI_PUBLIC_URL . On a closed network, use the widget.

# API, MCP and CLI · Smriti docs
URL: https://safearly.com/docs/api

API, MCP and CLI Everything in the web app is available over HTTP. Interactive OpenAPI docs are served by every installation at /api/docs . Authentication Demo mode uses the directory in the pack and a X-Smriti-User header. For local trials only. Token mode ( SMRITI_AUTH=token ) maps bearer tokens in SMRITI_API_TOKENS to people, behind your SSO proxy. Agent keys ( sk-smriti-… ) work only on that agent's chat endpoint and the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and act as their creator. Main endpoints Endpoint Use POST /api/ask , /api/ask/stream Ask the memory, with citations, verification and an optional "as of" date. GET /api/search Permission-aware search without an answer. GET /api/documents , /api/documents/{id} Documents, versions, diffs and access explanations. GET/POST /api/connectors , POST /api/ingest/upload Sources and uploads; /api/jobs for progress. GET /api/agents/catalog Kinds, tools, workflow steps, templates and expression functions. GET/POST/PUT/DELETE /api/agents Agents and workflows. POST /api/agents/{id}/chat Run an agent. Set stream for server-sent events. POST /api/agents/preview Run an unsaved agent or workflow. POST /api/runs/{id}/approve Approve or decline a paused action. GET/POST /api/tools Connected tools. GET/POST /api/channels Widget and chat integrations. GET /api/metrics , /api/health?deep=1 Prometheus metrics and readiness. Streaming events Streamed runs send these server-sent events: start (run and conversation ids), step (a retrieval, plan, tool call or workflow step), token (answer text), approval (paused until approved) and final (the verified answer, citations, steps and files). OpenAI-compatible from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI(base_url="https://smriti.example/v1", api_key="sk-smriti-…") r = client.chat.completions.create( model="agent/contract-analyst", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is the liability cap?"}], ) print(r.choices[0].message.content) Use the model smriti/<tenant> with a user token to ask the memory directly. The answer carries its sources. MCP server smriti mcp --as asha Exposes search_knowledge , ask_question and get_document to an MCP client, with the caller's permissions fixed when it starts. CLI Command Does smriti serve --seed Run the API and web app, seeding the demo on first start. smriti worker Run schedules and background jobs. smriti ingest , smriti crawl Ingest files or crawl a configured source. smriti ask Ask from the terminal. smriti eval gate Run the release gates. smriti bench Load-test a running server. smriti audit-verify Check the audit hash chain. smriti validate-pack Check a pack without starting anything. smriti sandbox Run the code-execution service.

# FAQ and limits · Smriti docs
URL: https://safearly.com/docs/faq

FAQ and limits Answers to the questions people ask most, and what the current release does not do yet. Questions Do I need a GPU? No. The CPU profile searches, quotes verified extracts, computes tables and runs research without a model. A GPU adds written answers and the full agentic tool loop. Can I use a hosted model instead? Yes. Point SMRITI_CHAT_URL at any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Personal data is masked before it is sent, but the provider will still see the rest of the prompt, so check that this fits your rules. Why did it say it can't answer? Either nothing you may read covers the question, or the draft answer failed verification. The steps panel shows which. Rephrase, check the sources the agent may use, or ask your knowledge manager whether the document is in the memory. Why do two people get different answers? Because they may read different documents. Every answer is built only from what the person asking may see. Does it work in languages other than English? Search, glossary expansion and the default embeddings and reranker are multilingual, and the demo includes Hindi questions. Check quality on your own golden set. How do I add my own domain checks? Write a skill in the pack: an extractor, rules in Python, templates and evaluation cases. See the skills folder of the demo pack. Limits of the current release OCR for scanned pages, advanced layout parsing and speech-to-text are plug-in points, not bundled. Scanned pages are flagged and queued. The 12 GB and 16 GB profiles are sized from arithmetic and haven't been run on those cards yet. Benchmark after install. OIDC single sign-on, fine-grained authorisation services and durable workflow engines are interfaces with local implementations. Adapters for live deployments still need to be written. OAuth connectors for cloud drives and workspace suites are on the roadmap. Release-gate numbers come from a small synthetic corpus. They show the gates work; measure accuracy on your own documents.

---

# Choosing a RAG stack for hard applications
URL: https://safearly.com/blog/rag-stack-case-study
Published: 2026-11-11

On this page Six applications, six retrieval problems Chunking Embeddings, every kind Choosing an embedding model Retrieval techniques Reranking Agentic RAG The combination per application What we measured The selection method Sources Blog / Case study Choosing a RAG stack for hard applications Lalit Shukla 11 Nov 2026 · Case study RAG Agentic RAG Embeddings Retrieval There is no best RAG pipeline, only the best one for a set of documents, questions and people. This case study shows how we choose each part of Smriti for six hard applications: how we chunk, which embeddings we use and why, how we retrieve, rerank and route to agents. For each choice we give what the published research supports and what we measured ourselves. The examples come from Smriti's demo library: a synthetic engineering and procurement office with contracts, amendments, tender notices, policy circulars in Hindi and English, a cost schedule spreadsheet, scanned letters and restricted audit files. Every number in the measured section can be reproduced with the open-source benchmark that ships with Smriti. Six applications, six retrieval problems Most RAG advice assumes one kind of question over one kind of document. Real offices have several, and each breaks a different part of the pipeline. Application What makes it hard The part that breaks first Contract and tender desk Answers turn on an exact clause, number or date; later amendments change earlier clauses Chunking that splits clauses; embeddings that blur "21 days" and "30 days" Multilingual policy helpdesk Questions in Hindi, documents in English, or the reverse; mixed scripts and transliteration Monolingual embedders and English-only keyword search Scanned and visual documents Letters, drawings, forms and tables where the layout carries the meaning Text extraction, before retrieval even starts Spreadsheets and registers Answers are aggregations ("total area in village Rampur"), not passages Treating rows as prose; the model doing arithmetic Investigations and chronologies The answer is spread across many documents and dates; some questions are about the whole collection Top-k retrieval, which finds passages but not patterns RTI and reply drafting Several sub-questions, each needing its own search, a legal deadline and exemptions to flag Single-shot RAG; it needs planning and tools Across all six there is a seventh requirement that is not negotiable: a person must never retrieve a passage from a document they are not allowed to open. That decides where filtering happens (inside the search, not after it) and rules out some techniques, which we point out as we go. Chunking: the decision that caps everything after it A retriever can only return what the chunker made. If a clause is split across two chunks, no embedding model or reranker will put it back together. These are the main families. Technique How it works Good for Watch out for Fixed-size with overlap Every N tokens, overlapping by 10 to 20% Uniform prose; a strong baseline Splits clauses, tables and lists mid-way Recursive Split on headings, then paragraphs, then sentences, until under the limit Most documents; the practical default Still blind to meaning inside a long section Structure-aware Use the document's own units: clause, section, article, row, slide, email Contracts, laws, policies, spreadsheets Needs a parser that understands the format Semantic Split where the embedding similarity between neighbouring sentences drops Transcripts and unstructured notes Costs an embedding pass; gains are inconsistent (below) Contextual headers Prefix each chunk with its document title, section path and date, or a generated summary of where it sits Any chunk that is ambiguous on its own ("the period shall be 21 days") A generated summary costs an LLM call per chunk at ingestion Late chunking Embed the whole document with a long-context model, then pool token vectors per chunk Chunks that depend on earlier context Needs a long-context embedder; modest gains Parent-child (small to big) Search small chunks, return their larger parent section to the model Precise matching with enough context to answer Larger prompts, so more prefill time Propositions An LLM rewrites text into atomic, self-contained facts Fact lookup over dense prose Expensive ingestion; the rewriting can introduce errors Page images No text chunks: embed each page image (see ColPali below) Visually rich pages, scans, slides Larger index; harder to cite a sentence The research is more sobering than the vendor blogs. A NAACL 2025 Findings study from Vectara compared semantic and fixed-size chunking on document retrieval, evidence retrieval and answer generation. It found the gains from semantic chunking were not consistent enough to justify its cost, and fixed-size chunking often did as well or better. Late chunking (Jina, 2024) gave small, consistent improvements on long-document retrieval benchmarks. The largest gain came from adding context to the chunk: Anthropic reported that contextual embeddings plus contextual BM25 cut failed top-20 retrievals by 49%, from 5.7% to 2.9%, and by 67% (to 1.9%) with a reranker added. What Smriti does Structure-aware chunking first: one chunk per numbered clause in contracts and codes, paragraph groups in circulars and letters, and for tables the whole table plus row groups that repeat the column names, with a structured copy kept for exact arithmetic. Anything still too long is split by sentence with one sentence of overlap. Every chunk is embedded with a short contextual header (title, reference number, date and section path), built from metadata at no LLM cost. Whether a rule has been superseded is metadata the search filters on, not text in the chunk. Embeddings, every kind "Embedding" covers several different representations with different strengths. A production stack usually combines two or three. Type Examples Strength Weakness Lexical sparse (BM25) Postgres full text, Qdrant sparse, Elasticsearch Exact terms: clause numbers, codes, names, amounts. Robust on new domains No synonyms, no cross-language matching Dense single-vector (bi-encoder) Qwen3-Embedding, BGE-M3, multilingual-e5, Nomic, Jina Meaning, paraphrase and cross-language matching; one fast vector search Blurs exact numbers and rare identifiers Learned sparse SPLADE, BGE-M3 sparse output Term weights with learned expansion; still an inverted index Mostly English-trained; larger index than BM25 Multi-vector, late interaction ColBERTv2, Jina-ColBERT, BGE-M3 multi-vector Token-level matching; strong quality, good for reranking One vector per token: much more storage Multimodal page embeddings ColPali, ColQwen Retrieves scanned and visual pages without OCR Storage per page; answers still need text to cite Matryoshka (variable size) Qwen3-Embedding (32 to 4,096 dims), Nomic, OpenAI v3 Truncate vectors to trade a little quality for memory Only for models trained that way Quantized vectors int8 (4× smaller), binary (32× smaller) Fit large collections in RAM Needs rescoring with full vectors to keep quality A few results shape how we use these. BEIR (NeurIPS 2021) showed that BM25 is a hard baseline to beat on new domains, and that dense models trained on one domain often fall behind it on another. ColBERT and ColBERTv2 showed that late interaction recovers much of a cross-encoder's quality at search time; ColBERTv2's residual compression cut its storage substantially. ColPali (ICLR 2025) embedded page images directly and beat text pipelines on visually rich documents, including pipelines that captioned every figure with a strong vision model. BGE-M3 produces dense, sparse and multi-vector outputs from one model across more than 100 languages. On quantization, int8 vectors with rescoring were lossless in Microsoft's Azure evaluation at about 75% less vector storage; binary vectors need a rescoring step to stay close. Choosing an embedding model The MTEB leaderboard (and its multilingual successor, MMTEB) is the place to start, and the wrong place to finish. Averages hide what matters for one deployment. We shortlist on six questions, in this order: Languages. Hindi, Tamil or Bengali questions over English documents need a model trained for cross-lingual retrieval, not just multilingual text. Check the retrieval tasks in your languages, not the overall average. Licence and weights. For an air-gapped install the weights must be downloadable and the licence must allow your use. Qwen3-Embedding, BGE-M3 and multilingual-e5 are open-weight and permissively licensed; check each model card. Memory and speed. The embedder shares a GPU with the LLM and reranker. A 0.6B model at FP16 needs about 1.2 GB for weights; an 8B model needs about 16 GB. Re-indexing a million chunks is a real job; measure it (below). Context length. Long chunks, parent sections and late chunking need 8k tokens or more. Instructions and prefixes. e5 needs "query:" and "passage:" prefixes; Qwen3-Embedding expects an instruction on queries. Getting this wrong costs more than choosing a slightly weaker model. Your golden set. The last word goes to recall@10 and MRR on your own questions, asked by your own users, with the permission filters on. The Qwen3 Embedding family (0.6B, 4B and 8B, Apache-2.0) is our default: the 8B model reported first place on the MMTEB multilingual leaderboard at release (70.58, June 2025), and the 0.6B model fits beside a 4B LLM on a 12 GB GPU. For CPU-only installs we use multilingual-e5-small. Both are swappable in one line of configuration, and the benchmark below is how we decide when to swap. Retrieval techniques Retrieval is everything between the question and the reranker. These are the techniques worth knowing, grouped by the problem they solve. Combining signals Hybrid search with reciprocal rank fusion. Run BM25 and dense search, then add 1/(k + rank) for each list a passage appears in (Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher, SIGIR 2009, with k = 60). It needs no score calibration and rarely does worse than either list. Weighted score fusion can rank better but must be tuned per collection. Filtering inside the search. Permissions, document type, date ranges and "current version only" are applied as filters in the index query, so the top-k is filled with passages the person may read. Filtering after retrieval returns fewer or no results and, worse, leaks timing and counts. Fixing the question Query rewriting. Expand abbreviations ("PG" to "performance guarantee"), resolve follow-ups ("and for works above that?") and translate. Cheap and effective. HyDE (Gao et al., ACL 2023). Generate a hypothetical answer and embed that instead of the question. It helps on zero-shot dense retrieval, but a wrong detail in the fake answer steers the search, so it is a probe, never evidence. Multi-query and RAG-Fusion. Ask several rephrasings and fuse their results with RRF. Raises recall on vague questions at the cost of more searches. Decomposition. Split a compound question into sub-questions, retrieve for each, then combine. This is where single-shot RAG starts turning into agentic RAG. Time and versions As-of retrieval and supersession. In regulated work the right answer is the rule in force on a date. Amendments and new circulars must mark what they replace, and retrieval must prefer the current version while still being able to answer "what was the rule in 2023?". No embedding model solves this; it is metadata. Structure across documents GraphRAG (Microsoft, 2024) extracts an entity graph, clusters it into communities and summarizes each, so it can answer whole-collection questions ("what are the main themes in these audit reports?") that top-k retrieval cannot. Indexing is expensive. LightRAG (2024) keeps a graph with dual-level retrieval and cheaper updates. RAPTOR (ICLR 2024) builds a tree of recursive summaries for questions at different levels of detail. Graph and summary indexes have a permission problem: a community summary mixes facts from documents with different access. Smriti does not build a cross-document graph or summary index today for this reason; any that are added must be built per access scope. Placing the context Order matters. "Lost in the middle" (TACL 2024) showed models use information at the start and end of a long context better than the middle. Send fewer, better passages, strongest first. Reranking: precision, not recall A reranker reads the question and each candidate together and scores how well the candidate answers it. It can only reorder what the first stage found; it cannot recover a passage the retriever missed. So the first stage is tuned for recall and the reranker for precision. Reranker Cost When Cross-encoder (bge-reranker-v2-m3, Qwen3-Reranker, mxbai) One forward pass per candidate; linear in candidates The default. Rerank 30 to 50 candidates, send the top 5 to 8 Late interaction (ColBERT) as reranker Cheap per candidate once token vectors exist When you already store multi-vector embeddings LLM listwise reranking An LLM call over all candidates Small candidate sets where reasoning matters more than latency Rules and metadata boosts Free Prefer current versions, exact clause matches, the asker's own division Reranking is also what lets you send less to the LLM. Five well-chosen passages produce a faster prefill and a better answer than fifteen loosely relevant ones. That makes the reranker one of the biggest levers on inference cost, not just quality. Agentic RAG: when one search is not enough Classic RAG retrieves once and answers. Agentic RAG lets the model decide whether to retrieve, what to search for next, which tool to use and when it has enough. The research has converged on a few patterns. Retrieve, reason, retrieve (ReAct, ICLR 2023). The model alternates thinking and tool calls. It handles multi-hop questions: find the tender, then its value, then the officer whose powers cover that value. Self-RAG (ICLR 2024) trains the model to decide when to retrieve and to critique its own output for support and relevance. Corrective RAG (2024) grades the retrieved passages and, when they are weak, rewrites the query or searches elsewhere before answering. Adaptive-RAG (NAACL 2024) classifies question complexity and routes each to no retrieval, single-step or multi-step retrieval, so easy questions stay cheap. The surveys (Singh et al., 2025) are clear that these patterns raise accuracy on complex questions and raise cost and latency with them. An agent that makes six searches and three LLM calls costs several times a single-shot answer. So routing is the most important agentic feature: in Smriti, lookup questions go to single-shot retrieval (often answered extractively, without the LLM at all), and only compound, comparative or drafting tasks go to an agent. The security rule for agents An agent's tools run with the permissions of the person asking, never the agent's own. Every search an agent makes is filtered exactly like a chat search, retrieved text is treated as untrusted data (it may contain injected instructions), and actions that change anything go through approval. See agents act as the asker . The combination per application Putting it together, this is the starting stack we use for each application. Each is a starting point to be checked against that application's golden set, not a fixed recipe. Application Chunking Retrieval Reranking and answer Contract and tender desk Clause-aware, with header (document, clause, date, superseded) Hybrid BM25 + dense with RRF; as-of filter; exact clause boost Cross-encoder; every sentence verified against its citation, numbers checked exactly Multilingual helpdesk Recursive, with header Multilingual dense (Qwen3 or e5) + BM25 per language; query translation Multilingual cross-encoder (bge-reranker-v2-m3); answer in the asker's language with original quotes Scanned and visual documents OCR or layout parsing to text; page images where layout matters Text hybrid, plus page-image retrieval (ColPali family) for visual pages Cross-encoder on text; low-confidence OCR flagged for review, never silently answered Spreadsheets and registers One chunk per row with column names, plus a table summary Hybrid to find the table; then a tool, not retrieval, for the numbers Agent with a calculator or sandboxed code; arithmetic done by code, not by the model Investigations and chronologies Recursive with dates extracted as metadata Multi-query, date-sorted retrieval; graph or summary index per access scope for collection-wide questions Research agent that plans sub-questions and marks gaps where an expected record is missing RTI and reply drafting Clause-aware, with header Decomposition: one search per point of the application Agent with a skill: deadline calculation, possible exemptions flagged for the officer to decide, draft for human signature What we measured We ran Smriti's benchmark on a laptop: an AMD Ryzen 7 7435HS (16 threads) with Docker given 12 GB of memory, and both embedding servers on CPU (Hugging Face Text Embeddings Inference 1.9). The library is the synthetic demo: 14 documents in English and Hindi, 39 chunks. These numbers show the method and the size of the trade-offs, not production capacity. 1. Embedding speed: the hidden cost of a bigger model Embedder on CPU, 350-token chunks Batch 1 Batch 8 Batch 32 1M chunks, best case multilingual-e5-small (118M, 384 dims) 3,714 tok/s 5,068 tok/s 5,552 tok/s about 24 hours Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (1,024 dims) 122 tok/s 72 tok/s 66 tok/s about 56 days The small model was 30 to 85 times faster, and the larger model got slower with bigger batches on this CPU backend. A model that is fine for embedding one question at a time can be unusable for re-indexing a library. That is why Smriti's CPU and 6 GB profiles use e5-small and keep Qwen3-Embedding for GPU profiles. 2. The golden set could not tell the models apart Embedder (hybrid with BM25, built-in reranker) Golden set Recall@10 MRR Leaks Index 39 chunks Per question Hashing (built in, no model) 14/14 1.0 1.0 0 0.7 s 12 ms multilingual-e5-small 14/14 1.0 1.0 0 1.7 s 37 ms Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B 14/14 1.0 1.0 0 49.5 s 379 ms Every combination passed, including a hashing embedder with no neural model at all. The golden questions use the documents' own words (clause numbers, tender numbers, "performance guarantee"), and BM25 plus the contextual headers finds them on its own. That is good news for the product and bad news for model selection: a saturated test cannot choose a model. 3. Hard questions separate them So we wrote ten harder questions that avoid the documents' wording: paraphrases ("how long does a firm get to hand in its bank guarantee after it wins the work?") and cross-language questions (Hindi questions about English documents, an English question about a Hindi circular). We scored each setup on the same 39 chunks, fusing the lists the way Smriti does (top 20 of each, reciprocal rank fusion with k = 60). Setup, 10 hard questions Right document first In top 5 MRR Cross-language, top 5 BM25 only 4 5 0.47 0 of 4 multilingual-e5-small, dense only 9 10 0.93 4 of 4 multilingual-e5-small + BM25 (RRF) 7 9 0.81 3 of 4 Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, dense only 7 10 0.79 4 of 4 Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B + BM25 (RRF) 6 8 0.73 2 of 4 Four lessons, with the caveat that ten questions over 39 chunks is a small sample: Keyword search cannot cross languages. BM25 found none of the cross-language answers; both dense models found all four. Hybrid is not free. Equal-weight fusion helps when the question shares the document's words (the golden set) and hurts when it does not: BM25 adds confident-looking noise. The fix is not to drop BM25, which wins on clause numbers and codes, but to put a cross-encoder after fusion, weight the lists by query type, or skip BM25 when the question and documents are in different scripts. That is our next measurement. Bigger was not better here. The 118M-parameter model beat the 0.6B model on first-place hits at a fraction of the compute. On a sample this small the difference is not significant; the point is that the leaderboard ranking did not carry over, so it has to be measured on your own data. Measure the model and its prefixes together. Both models need the right query instructions ("query:" for e5, an instruction for Qwen3). The first version of our own benchmark silently dropped the Qwen3 instruction; a test now guards it. 4. The LLM on a 6 GB laptop GPU The same tool sweeps an LLM server across 1, 2, 4 and 8 simultaneous users and reports time to first token, time per token, throughput and goodput against a latency target. We ran Qwen3-4B (4-bit Q4_K_M) on llama.cpp on the laptop's RTX 4050 with 6 GB of memory, with RAG-shaped prompts of about 1,450 tokens and answers of up to 256. The target: first token within 2 seconds and under 100 ms per token after that, for 90% of requests. Configuration Memory One user 8 users, total Users within target Qwen3-4B, 8-bit KV cache 4.6 GB 53 tok/s 104 tok/s 2 Qwen3-4B, 16-bit KV cache 5.6 GB 57 tok/s 83 tok/s 2 Qwen3-4B, 8-bit KV, 1,000-token prompts 4.7 GB 51 tok/s 113 tok/s 4 Qwen3-4B, 8-bit KV, shared prompt prefix 4.7 GB 54 tok/s 163 tok/s 8 Qwen3-1.7B (8-bit), 8-bit KV cache 3.9 GB 76 tok/s 110 tok/s 8 This ties back to retrieval. On a small GPU the limit was not generating the answer but reading the prompt: every new 1,450-token prompt paused everyone else's answer for about 0.7 seconds. Two changes fixed most of it, and both are retrieval decisions. Sending 1,000 tokens of better-chosen passages instead of 1,450 doubled the users served within target. Keeping the start of the prompt identical across requests, so the server reuses its cached work, took it to 8 users and cut the first token to 27 ms for a single user. A smaller model was faster for one person but no better under load. Better reranking is how you send fewer tokens, which makes it an inference optimization as much as a quality one. Smriti's 6 GB profile now uses these settings: llama.cpp with the 4-bit model, an 8-bit KV cache, 1,000 tokens of context and 4 concurrent answers. Larger cards run vLLM; we will publish those numbers with the commands to reproduce them. The selection method Every choice above comes from the same loop, and Smriti ships the tools for each step. Write the golden set first. Real questions, the person asking, the date, the documents that should be found and the ones that must not. Include questions that should be refused. Smriti packs keep it in evals/golden.yaml . Measure retrieval alone. Recall@10 and MRR with the LLM switched off. If the right passage is not retrieved, no model can answer from it. smriti modelbench retrieval runs every embedder and reranker combination. Then measure answers. Faithfulness, citation precision and correct refusals; RAGAS-style metrics help, but we check citations and numbers with code, not only with a judge model. Gate on security. Zero leaks on the permission suite and a passing red team, on every change. A better model that leaks is not better. Measure cost last, not never. Embedding throughput for re-indexing, reranker latency per candidate count, and LLM goodput at your latency target, with smriti modelbench embed , rerank and chat . The tools are open source in the Smriti repository , with a tuning guide that lists every serving knob in the order we change them. Sources Anthropic, Introducing Contextual Retrieval , 2024. # Weight-space programming, explained: when an LLM edits a neural network's weights
URL: https://safearly.com/blog/weight-space-programming
Published: 2026-11-09

On this page What it is What was shown The caveats The auditing angle What it means for teams Sources Blog / Explainer Weight-space programming, explained: when an LLM edits a neural network's weights Lalit Shukla 9 Nov 2026 · Explainer Research Interpretability AI safety For as long as there have been neural networks, the only practical way to change one has been to train it. A new piece of research suggests a second way: hand the weights to a language model, describe what you want, and let it rewrite the numbers. What it is Weight-space programming means a general-purpose language model reads a neural network's raw weights, works out what the network does, and edits or writes those weights directly. There is no optimizer and no gradient descent, and in some experiments no feedback from running the network at all. The weights are treated less like the output of training and more like source code a capable reader can inspect and change. The term comes from "Sparks of Weight-Space Programming", published on 2 November 2026 by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab of MIT CSAIL. The work is a research write-up and has not been peer-reviewed. Training changes weights through data and millions of small steps. Weight-space programming has a model read them and change a few values on purpose. What was shown The experiments used one frontier model, which the authors call Astra, on networks that are tiny by today's standards. The results that drew attention: Reading. Given only the weights of four small game-playing policies (about 17,000 weights each), it named the game each one had learned to play. Given three small character-level language models, it named the language each was trained on and found the attention heads that copy text. Editing. A 171,664-weight policy that never got a car up a ramp in 256 attempts was changed by one edit to 3.5% of its weights. The edited policy succeeded in all 1,024 test episodes. Writing from scratch. With no training at all, it wrote a Breakout policy that scored 517.4, against 25.3 for a standard reinforcement-learning baseline trained for 500 million steps. On two other games the hand-written policies came close to, but did not beat, the trained ones. A small real language model. Changing 131,072 weights in Qwen3.5-0.8B (0.016%) raised its MATH-500 score from 7.9% to 48.1% and GSM8K from 13.8% to 67.1%. The edit removed one direction from two layers' outputs, which mostly stopped the model from running past its token limit. The caveats This is early work, and the authors say so. The details matter more than the headlines: Small networks. The reading and editing results without tools were on networks of roughly 17,000 to 172,000 weights. Frontier models have hundreds of billions. Not always tool-free. The Go and Qwen experiments allowed a Python sandbox and dozens of forward passes, so they are closer to assisted research than pure reading. Nothing new was added. The authors write that edits could remove an obstacle hiding an ability, but not add one the model lacked. Critics note a skilled researcher could likely have found the Qwen fix. It failed too. It could not find the cause of sycophancy in Gemma 3 270M from weights alone, and edits to that model's maths ability made no meaningful difference. Not yet replicated by an independent group. The auditing angle The most interesting follow-up so far is about checking networks, not improving them. A preprint posted on 3 November 2026 by Humza Nusrat and Omar Nusrat applied the idea to small clinical decision networks (433 to 4,801 parameters) that screen radiotherapy requests against four rules. They planted flaws: confounds that hid a rule, a shifted dose threshold, and a hidden trigger, a stand-in for a backdoor. A frontier model then audited each network blind, with no data or code execution, and every claim was tested on about 420,000 requests. It named the broken rule in 16 of 18 flawed networks and repaired all 16 by changing a median of three parameters, where fine-tuning changed nearly all of them. But it found only one of the three hidden triggers, and it wrongly failed some healthy networks. The authors' own conclusion is the right one to quote: it can locate and repair these flaws in small networks, but cannot yet certify that a network is correct. What it means for teams shipping AI Weights are editable, so verify them. If a capable model can make targeted, hard-to-spot edits to weights, then a downloaded model is only as trustworthy as its provenance. Pin checksums, record where every model came from, and re-run your evaluations after any change. Don't trust a model's behaviour, test it. Weight-space auditing missed most hidden triggers. Behavioural evaluation on your own data, red-team sets and leakage tests remain the evidence that counts. Keep guarantees outside the model. Whatever happens inside the weights, access control, verification of answers against sources, and approval for actions should not depend on the model behaving. That is the principle we build Smriti on. Weight-space programming may become a real interpretability and repair tool. For now it is a striking demonstration on small networks, and a useful reminder that model weights are an attack surface as well as an asset. Sources Takehi, Teoh, Zhang and Khattab (MIT CSAIL), Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights , 2 Nov 2026. Nusrat and Nusrat, Weight-space programming for auditing clinical decision networks (arXiv 2611.05341), 3 Nov 2026. The Register, Forget retraining: AI can now tweak another AI's weights , 3 Nov 2026. Wikipedia, Weight-space programming , including summaries of published critiques. Figures are quoted from the sources above as of 9 November 2026. The work is recent and unreplicated; we'll update this post as it develops. Essay Agent Skills is now an open standard Research note Check every sentence, not just the answer
